title: House Robber
summary: You can't rob two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can rob.
statement:
Houses along a street contain `nums[i]` money each. You cannot rob two adjacent houses, because the alarm would go off.

Return the maximum amount of money you can rob.
hints: At each house you either rob it or skip it.
best[i] = max(best[i − 1], best[i − 2] + nums[i]): skip house i, or rob it on top of the best up to i − 2.
Only the last two values are needed, so keep two variables.

title: House Robber II
summary: The houses form a circle, so the first and last are adjacent. You can't rob two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can rob.
statement:
As in "House Robber", but the houses are arranged in a circle: the first house and the last house are neighbours. You still cannot rob two adjacent houses.

Return the maximum amount of money you can rob.
hints: The circle only adds one conflict: the first and last houses cannot both be robbed.
So either the first house is skipped or the last house is skipped.
Run the linear House Robber on nums[0..n−2] and on nums[1..n−1] and take the larger result. A single house is a special case.

title: Maximum Subarray
summary: Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray.
statement:
Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums`.

If every value is negative, the answer is the largest single value.
hints: For each index, what is the best subarray that ends exactly there?
Kadane's algorithm: bestEndingHere = max(nums[i], bestEndingHere + nums[i]). A negative running sum is never worth keeping.
Track the maximum of bestEndingHere over all i. Start both with nums[0] to handle all-negative arrays.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
summary: Return the largest product of any non-empty contiguous subarray.
statement:
Return the largest product of any non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums`.

The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: Every subarray product fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Unlike sums, a very negative product can turn into the largest one when multiplied by another negative number.
Track both the maximum and the minimum product of a subarray ending at each index.
For each value x: newMax = max(x, x·max, x·min) and newMin = min(x, x·max, x·min), computed from the old values. A zero resets both.

title: Decode Ways
summary: Letters map to "1".."26". Return how many ways the digit string can be decoded ("06" is not a valid code).
statement:
Letters are encoded as numbers: `A` → `"1"`, `B` → `"2"`, …, `Z` → `"26"`. Given a string of digits `s`, return the number of ways to decode it back into letters.

A piece with a leading zero, such as `"06"`, is not a valid code. If the string cannot be decoded at all, return `0`. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: `s` has only digits and may contain leading zeros
hints: The last letter of a decoding uses either the last one digit or the last two digits.
ways[i] = (ways[i − 1] if s[i − 1] is 1–9) + (ways[i − 2] if s[i − 2..i − 1] is 10–26), with ways[0] = 1.
Zeros are the trap: "0" alone is never valid, so "30" decodes zero ways. Two variables are enough.

title: Word Break
summary: Return whether s can be split into a sequence of dictionary words (words may be reused).

perf.label: a 151-character string
perf.gen: String a0 = "a".repeat(150) + "b"; List<String> a1 = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) a1.add("a".repeat(i));

statement: Return `true` if `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more words from `wordDict`. The same dictionary word may be used many times.
constraints: All strings are lowercase; dictionary words are unique
hints: Trying every split recursively explodes on inputs like "aaaa…ab". The same suffix gets solved again and again.
Let ok[i] mean "the first i characters can be split". ok[0] is true.
ok[i] is true if some j < i has ok[j] and s[j..i) in the dictionary (use a HashSet, and only try lengths up to the longest word).

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
summary: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence — O(n log n) if you can.
statement:
Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of `nums`. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements.

The O(n²) dynamic programming solution is fine for these sizes; an O(n log n) solution exists.
hints: Let lis[i] be the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i.
lis[i] = 1 + max(lis[j]) over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]. That is O(n²).
For O(n log n), keep tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1, and binary-search where each value goes.

title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
summary: Return how many longest strictly increasing subsequences there are.
statement:
Return how many strictly increasing subsequences of `nums` have the maximum possible length.

Subsequences are counted by the positions they use, so equal values at different positions make different subsequences. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Extend the O(n²) LIS solution: alongside length[i], track count[i], the number of longest subsequences ending at i.
For j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: if length[j] + 1 is longer than length[i], take over count[j]; if it is equal, add count[j].
At the end, add up count[i] for every i whose length equals the overall maximum.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
summary: Trade as often as you like (one share at a time), but after selling you must skip the next day. Return the maximum profit.
statement:
`prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. You may make as many trades as you like, holding at most one share at a time, but after you sell you must wait one day (a cooldown) before you can buy again.

Return the maximum profit.
hints: Describe each day by your state: holding a share, just sold (cooling down), or free to buy.
hold = max(hold, free − price); sold = hold + price; free = max(free, previous sold). Compute the new values from the old ones.
The answer is max(sold, free) after the last day.

title: Russian Doll Envelopes
summary: An envelope fits into another only if both its width and height are strictly smaller. Return the most envelopes you can nest.

perf.label: 100,000 envelopes
perf.gen: int[][] a0 = new int[100000][]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = new int[] { BCB.rnd(1, 100000), BCB.rnd(1, 100000) };

statement:
`envelopes[i] = [width, height]`. One envelope fits inside another only if both its width and its height are strictly smaller. Envelopes cannot be rotated.

Return the maximum number of envelopes you can nest one inside the other.
hints: Sort by width; then you need an increasing subsequence of heights. Equal widths are the catch.
Sort by width ascending and, for equal widths, by height descending. Then two envelopes of the same width can never both be in an increasing run of heights.
Run the O(n log n) longest increasing subsequence on the heights; O(n²) is too slow for 10⁵ envelopes.
